title: The Larger Catechism and the Lord's Supper - Part 2
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
series: The Larger Catechism and the Lord's Supper
summary: This lesson explores questions 163-164 and 168 from the Larger Catechism, focusing on the nature and components of sacraments and defining the Lord's Supper. The teaching emphasizes both the physical and spiritual dimensions of sacramental participation and explains how the Lord's Supper functions as a means of grace that confirms believers' union with Christ and one another.

outline.title: Background and Context of the Larger Catechism
subpoints: The Larger Catechism was written in the 1640s by the Westminster Assembly
Adopted by Scotland in 1648 as a directory for catechizing those with proficiency in religion
Part of the denominational constitution and standards for Presbyterian churches worldwide
Designed for adult Christian education, not just memorization

outline.title: Question 164: How Many Sacraments Has Christ Instituted?
subpoints: Christ instituted only two sacraments in the New Testament: baptism and the Lord's Supper
This contrasts with Roman Catholic teaching of seven sacraments
All Old Testament rituals have been fulfilled in Christ and are no longer required
Baptism and the Lord's Supper are the primary means through which God dispenses grace

outline.title: Question 163: The Two Parts of a Sacrament
subpoints: An outward and sensible sign used according to Christ's appointment
An inward and spiritual grace signified by that sign
Physical performance is essential—merely thinking about the elements is insufficient
Both the physical act and spiritual reality must be present for a valid sacrament
Grace is conveyed by the Holy Spirit through the divinely appointed means

outline.title: Question 168: What Is the Lord's Supper?
subpoints: A sacrament of the New Testament instituted by Christ on the night before His death
Involves both bread and wine according to Christ's appointment
Proclaims Christ's death as atonement and His future return
Provides spiritual nourishment and growth in grace through faith and remembrance

outline.title: The Dual Historical and Eschatological Character of the Lord's Supper
subpoints: Looks backward to Christ's death and atonement for sin
Looks forward to Christ's future return and the consummation
Celebrates the entire period between crucifixion and return
Functions as a proclamation of the gospel in visible form

outline.title: The Lord's Supper as a Means of Grace and Covenant Renewal
subpoints: Provides spiritual nourishment through remembrance and faith in Christ's redemptive work
Confirms union and communion with Christ and fellow believers
Renews mutual love and fellowship as members of Christ's body
Weekly renewal of covenant commitment to God and obedience
Baptism is entry into covenant; the Lord's Supper is covenant renewal

outline.title: Requirements for Worthy Participation in the Lord's Supper
subpoints: Must partake in a worthy manner—only through faith in Christ
Must be able to examine oneself, implying belief in Christ
Must discern the body—understand the church and one's relationship to it
Requires credible profession of faith and church membership
Not permitted for children without profession of faith
Protection against unworthy partaking and judgment

transcript:
## Background of the Larger Catechism

We are currently considering the Lord's Supper as taught in the Larger Catechism. This started from a question that was raised, and I thought it would be something good for all of us to consider. Let me remind you of the background of the Larger Catechism.

Remember there is a Westminster Confession and the Shorter Catechism and the Larger Catechism. They are all parts of our constitution—the theological portion of our denominational constitution. When elders and deacons are ordained, their oath of office is to uphold the system of doctrines outlined in the Westminster Confession and Catechisms, or as it is known, the Westminster Standards.

The catechisms were written long ago in the 1640s. After a lot of fighting in England and Scotland, they signed a Solemn League and Covenant in 1643, which stated that both countries would endeavor to bring the churches of God in the three kingdoms—England, Scotland, and Ireland—to the nearest conjunction and uniformity in religion, Confession of faith, form of church government, directory of worship, and catechizing, so that we and our posterity after us as brethren live in faith and love, and the Lord make delight to dwell in the midst of us.

Now that never materialized. England never left Scotland or Ireland alone. They kept on fighting. A deal was needed between Scotland and England because Charles I was running out of money to fight the war because he would not open Parliament. But that is what gave rise to the assembly. Shortly after that, the assembly was called to meet in Westminster, which is just across the way from Parliament, and they met there at the Abbey.

When the Westminster Assembly was established by the English Parliament, it took the responsibility for preparing the catechisms very seriously. As Christians are known to do, there was a lot of debate. For four years before any catechism was written—from 1643 to 1647—they debated about catechisms. In 1647, the assembly decided to write not one but two catechisms. That made the work a little easier because they could write one for children, which is what we call the Shorter Catechism, and then one for adults, which is what we call the Larger Catechism. That made their job a little simpler. So they moved that the committee for the catechisms prepare a draft of two catechisms: one more large and another more brief, in which they are to have an eye to the Confession of Faith and to the matter of catechism already begun.

Just a year later, they were able to produce the catechisms because they had already done so much work. They just had to organize things in 1648. They produced the catechisms, and the January assembly of Scotland adopted them right away. England never adopted the standards, but Scotland did. Scotland called the Larger Catechism a directory for catechizing such as have made some proficiency in the knowledge of the grounds of religion. So if you are just a little more than a baby in Christ, you would be ready to memorize the Larger Catechism. That is what is meant by having made some proficiency in the grounds of religion.

Things have changed, right? Quite a bit. We do not memorize much. We even think that memorizing the Shorter Catechism is something you do at seminary at the highest level of education, and that was not what was intended. So that is just the background that led to the writing of the Larger Catechism. It is adopted almost universally by every Presbyterian Bible-believing church in the world—not just the English-speaking world, but in the world. It is also part of the standards of the Bible Presbyterian church.

## Review: What Is a Sacrament?

Last time we were together, we looked at this one question: What is a sacrament?

> A sacrament is an holy ordinance instituted by Christ in his church to signify, seal, and exhibit unto those that are within the covenant of grace, the benefits of his mediation, to strengthen and increase their faith in all other graces, to oblige them to obedience, to testify and cherish their love and communion one with another, and to distinguish them from those that are without.

The assembly men did not like periods. They just do not use them. They use semicolons throughout the questions. If you missed last time, you can listen to that lesson on our website, on one of our podcasts, or in the OBPC lessons.

## Tonight's Focus

Tonight we are going to try to look at three questions. Two of them are general questions about the sacrament that we should be able to address pretty quickly. Then we are going to actually talk about the one that asks what is the Lord's Supper, which is actually the subject of our study. We are going to start with question 163. Tonight we are going to do 163, 164, and, the Lord willing, 168. But we are going to do 164 before 163 because I think it is easier, so we are just going to get that out of the way.

## Question 164: How Many Sacraments Has Christ Instituted?

Question 164 asks: How many sacraments has Christ instituted in this church and the New Testament?

The answer is: Under the New Testament, Christ has instituted in his church only two sacraments—baptism and the Lord's Supper.

That should be straightforward. We do not need a lot of explanation. This answer stands in stark opposition to the Roman Catholic teaching that there are seven sacraments. We believe the Bible teaches there are only two.

The New Testament clearly sets up these two ordinances together with preaching the Bible and praying in communion with the saints as means through which God dispenses grace to His people. So we have baptism and the Lord's Supper. There are no other rituals prescribed to the church in the New Testament other than baptism and the Lord's Supper. All of the Old Testament rituals have been fulfilled in Christ. That is why we do not practice them. That is why we do not sacrifice animals. That is why we do not have a period of purification after a woman gives birth. We do not do those things that are in the Old Testament because the book of Hebrews tells us that all those things have been fulfilled in Christ. So they are not for us. These are the only two things left for us.

## Question 163: What Are the Parts of a Sacrament?

Question 163 asks: What are the parts of a sacrament?

The answer is: The parts of a sacrament are two: the one an outward and sensible sign, used according to Christ's own appointment, the other an inward and spiritual grace thereby signified.

There is a physical aspect of the sacrament and a spiritual aspect in the sacrament. And it is also saying that in order to partake of a sacrament—in order to call the thing that you are doing a sacrament—you have to actually do it. That is what it means by an outward sensible sign. Sensible here does not mean reasonable. That is how we use the word sensible today. It means perceived by the senses—so physical, something you can touch, see, hear, smell, feel.

Just thinking, for example, about the water, just thinking about the bread, just thinking about the wine is not the sacrament. The actual pouring of water on the head in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit needs to happen in order to be a sacrament. The actual eating of the bread and drinking of the wine together with the saints needs to happen in order to be a sacrament. That is why that first half of the question addresses the physical side. Without the physical side, you do not have a sacrament.

Notice that it is not a minor detail. This is not a minor detail. It is according to Christ's own appointment. Doing the sacraments correctly is important because Christ appointed the way to do it. He did not say, just go figure out whatever you want. Crackers and apple juice, or somebody using whatever they have in the house and whatever liquid they can drink—that is not going to be the Lord's Supper. Christ appointed it particularly. That is why we are so particular about how we do things here. We are trying to follow Christ's own appointment of the sacraments.

So physically doing the thing that Christ has appointed is necessary for it to be a sacrament. Just thinking about the order, just thinking about the bread, just thinking about the cup—that is not enough. You need to do it.

Think with me for a moment. Remember the occasion when the angel of the Lord was chasing Moses as he traveled with his two boys, threatening to kill them. It was not enough for Moses just to think about circumcising his boys. He had to do it. And it had to be done in a hurry; otherwise, the angel of the Lord was going to kill them.

Paul then asked the Ephesians in Acts 19. He finds disciples in Ephesus and asked them, have you been baptized? They say no. He does not say, just think really hard about water and you will be baptized. No, he actually baptizes them. The same with the unbelievers in Corinth. They were not getting sick and dying because they were just thinking about the bread and the wine. They were actually partaking of the bread and the wine. That is why they were getting sick. So there is something important in the physicality of the sacraments.

By the end of the day, in order for the thing we are doing to be a sacrament, faith and grace need to be present—not just the physical but the spiritual as well. It is not just the eating of the bread. It is not just the drinking of the wine. It is not just having water poured on you that makes the sacraments. There has to be a spiritual reality to it as well.

The pouring of the water by itself, apart from the significance of the pouring of the water—namely, in grafting into Christ—is not a sacrament. Eating the bread and drinking the wine apart from the significance of the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ is not a sacrament. It is a happy hour. It is not a sacrament because there is no spiritual reality to it. The water, the bread, and the wine are important because they signify something. And as one partakes of these elements in faith in Jesus Christ, God conveys to them the grace associated with what they signify. Both the physical and the spiritual need to be there. It is not based on my faith, it is based on your faith, it is based on the work of the Spirit in your heart as you receive the sacraments.

### On the Connection Between Sign and Grace

Here is a long quote from Johannes Vos's commentary on the Larger Catechism:

> That is to say, by Christ's appointment, when the outward sign is rightly used with true faith, the spiritual grace which it stands for is actually given or conveyed to the recipient. God by his Holy Spirit distills the grace on the person who uses the outward sign aright. So in this sense, we may affirm that there is an instrumental connection between the sign and the grace. The grace is conveyed not by the sacrament of itself, but by the Holy Spirit. But inasmuch as the sacrament is a divinely appointed means of grace, the Holy Spirit honors it by bestowing the grace where the sacrament is used.

So where people are partaking of the sacrament correctly, where they are doing that in faith in Jesus Christ, God does give grace to those receiving. When it is done in faith and done correctly, there is a union between the elements and the grace of God that is brought about by faith. Paul is clear about that in Romans 4, where we talked about Abraham's circumcision being a means of grace to him because he did that in faith. In Romans 6, he speaks about baptism when it is done properly.

So there are these two elements: both the physical and the spiritual need to be present in order for it to be a sacrament.

## Question 168: What Is the Lord's Supper?

Question 168 asks: What is the Lord's Supper?

The answer is: The Lord's Supper is a sacrament of the New Testament, wherein, by giving and receiving bread and wine according to the appointment of Jesus Christ, His death is showed forth. And they that worthily communicate feed upon his body and blood to their spiritual nourishment and growth in grace, have their union and communion with him confirmed, testify and renew their thankfulness and engagement to God, and their mutual love and fellowship each with other as members of the same mystical body.

That is what the Lord's Supper is. First, it says this is a sacrament of the New Testament. What does that mean? It is describing a scripture in the New Testament. Though it was typified in the Passover, it was not instituted until the night before Jesus died.

In 1 Corinthians 11:23-25, Paul says:

> For I received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you: the Lord Jesus, on the same night in which he was betrayed, took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, "Take, eat, this is my body which is broken for you. Do this in remembrance of me." In the same manner, he also took the cup after supper, saying, "This cup is the new covenant in my blood. This do as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me."

So it is revealed in the New Testament. But it is also a New Covenant sacrament as opposed to an Old Covenant sacrament.

That next bolded and underlined part says it involves both bread and wine. I do not think we have to spend a lot of time talking about that—whether you want to say it is wine or grape juice, but it involves bread and the fruit of the grape. There was a whole series on this a few years ago and why we use alcohol and so on. What is important is that just having one of the elements is not the Lord's Supper. Just eating the bread or just drinking the cup is not the Lord's Supper. Bread and wine must be present for it to be the Lord's Supper. That is why sometimes we encourage people who got the bread but then had to get up because of a baby or whatever—they can come down the hall to get the other elements so they can protect the whole sacrament, not just part of it.

### The Proclamation of Christ's Death and Future Return

The definition continues and says it proclaims Christ's death as an atonement for the sins of His people and His future return for His people. That is what the Lord's Supper does.

We see that in 1 Corinthians 11:26:

> For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.

He proclaims the death—that is the atonement part for His people. He comes—that is His future return. So there is a historical element to the Lord's Supper, looking back to the death of Christ, but there is also a eschatological element. We are looking forward to the coming of Christ. The Lord's Supper celebrates this entire period between the crucifixion and the return of Christ. And it is a means of sanctifying grace.

It says it provides spiritual nourishment and growth in grace. How does the Lord's Supper do that? As we partake of that bread, remembering that Christ's body was broken for us, we grow in grace. And the same thing we do when we take that cup—we recognize that Christ, by faith, as a payment and word of redemption for us. And we are trying to be his people.

As we think about what was taken to that, yes, and it converts our faith in the very God, and it converts grace for us. Yes, it is quite remarkable. It is because Christ said it is. It is an establishment of grace. But when he says, you do this and I will spiritually meet with my people in this way. Now, there is nothing special in it of itself except that that is what Christ said he was going to do. So it is.

I am asking this question because there is no verse you can go to that explicitly says, "And the Lord's Supper is a means of grace." There is no verse you can go to that explicitly says, "As you do this, God is going to spend grace." But it is in the teaching of the scriptures.

I was thinking specifically, as you remember Christ, as you hold down to Christ, as you are partaking of the Lord's Supper—and the Heidelberg Catechism was super helpful in this—"As real as this bread that I hold in my hand is, so real is Christ's death for me on the cross." That is all part of remembering Christ. That is what we are doing in 1 Corinthians 11:24-25, remembering Christ.

So in that way, then, the Lord's Supper becomes a means of grace. As you focus on Christ in partaking of the elements, then that becomes a means of grace. If you remember, my prayer almost every Sunday, when we sanctify the bread and the cup, is: "Lord, bless this bread to our souls because as we partake of it in faith in Christ"—that is the only way that, as we remember Christ in that context, that becomes a means of grace.

### Union and Communion with Christ and One Another

It also says it confirms our union and communion with Christ and one another. First Corinthians 10:13-16 says:

> The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?

We often stay in 1 Corinthians 11 for the Lord's Supper, but 1 Corinthians 10 has a lot to teach concerning the Lord's Supper. The idea is that as we partake of it, as we eat the bread, there is a significant element—the idea that if you go to that time, one loaf was used for the Lord's Supper. Every piece of bread came from the same loaf. Now we use sliced bread, and it is different. But normally speaking, they all came from one loaf because of this concept that we are partaking together. The body is one loaf, and we are eating of that same loaf—union with each other. It also indicates covenant renewal.

By partaking of the Lord's Supper, believers show and renew their mutual love and fellowship as members of Christ's spiritual body, the church. So it is not just me and Jesus. It is us and Jesus. Some people say, "Oh, we should look around." I know that is awkward. But it is not a chatty time; it is not a "hey, how are you?" time. But it is not just me and Jesus and nobody else. It is us and Jesus. It is a renewal ceremony. Baptism is your entry into covenant with God. The Lord's Supper is renewing weekly that covenant that we have with God. It also involves a renewal of our covenant commitment of love and obedience to God.

Again, in 1 Corinthians 10:14-17, Paul says:

> Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to sensible men; judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we, though many, are one body, one bread, for we are all partakers of that one bread. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the Lord's table and of the table of demons.

And lastly, the catechism speaks of the manner of our taking, saying that we are to partake worthily. They that worthily communicate feed upon his body and his blood. The Lord's Supper is for those who have a credible profession of faith. That is what "worthily" means here.

## Worthy Participation in the Lord's Supper

In 1 Corinthians 11:27-29, Paul says:

> Therefore, whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of the body and the blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy manner eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.

Notice Paul says three things about those that are to partake of the Supper in these verses.

First, in verse 27, they must do it in a worthy manner. And the only worthy way is in Christ. So when it says "worthily" here, it does not say, "Look at your works and look how good you have been this week. Look at whatever all the good things you have done." No, because your best works of righteousness are what in the sight of God? Filthy rags. So the best thing you can offer to God is, "God, look, look at all the filthy rags that brought you." I interpret please with me. So partaking worthily has nothing to do with that. It has to do with who Christ is. And the means are you in Christ through faith.

Secondly, in verse 28, one must be able to examine himself. Implied in that is that he is in Christ. Here is the in-Christ-ness represented by unity. So you have to be in Christ. You have to be able to examine yourself.

Thirdly, in verse 29, one must discern the body. The body here is the church. One must be able to evaluate his relationship to the church. And that is why we say that membership in the local church is so important in order to take the Lord's Supper. Because if you are not really discerning the body, you really do not understand the church if you choose to not be a member of a local church.

And these three activities can only be done—this idea of worthily can only be done—through faith in Christ. And they do require a certain level of cognitive ability. When I say that, that is why we require a credible profession of faith. You cannot take the Lord's Supper without a profession. That is why we do not allow children without a profession of faith to the table. We do not say an original image, but they do have to come to the elders and explain at some level what it means to believe in Christ. We interview the parents. Does it look like they have a credible faith at home? And so on? And that is what it means to partake worthily.

## Questions and Discussion

Does anyone have questions?

One question raised: If you have assurance, you cannot lose your salvation, then what is there to examine each week?

The examining is part of the way that you persevere to the end. When you examine yourself, you are not just examining yourself; you are also examining Christ's work on your behalf. If you stop at just looking at your heart, then you are doomed. So you also examine Christ's work for you. And as you do that, that is one of the means that God carries you to the end to persevere to the end. The same way that we need people in our lives helping us see what our blind spots are, we need to examine ourselves so that we can arrive at the end.

## Conclusion

The Lord's Office is a gracious gift from our Lord to help us grow in him and to grow into the clear knowledge of who he is. Our Lord knows that we are physical people. So he gives us this very sensual means—something that we can perceive by our senses. Not only does the preached word bring salvation to people, but the visible word of the Lord's Office also brings sanctification to people. It is a great gracious gift from our Father.
